newsitem.title: PERU: Rebels would rather stay in Peru than take asylum.
newsitem.headline: Rebels would rather stay in Peru than take asylum.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the besieged Japanese ambassador's home in Lima poured cold water on Tuesday on a proposal to win them asylum abroad in return for a peaceful end to the 77-day crisis.

Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa insisted the rebels want to stay in Peru and urged the government to concentrate instead on their principal demand for the freedom of some 400 jailed comrades.

"Our first priority is to stay in our fatherland, which is the path we have chosen to fight at the side of our people," Cerpa said in a walkie-talkie conversation from within the residence monitored by Reuters.
Cerpa specifically ruled out a rumoured asylum deal involving the Dominican Republic, but drew short of rejecting Cuban President Fidel Castro's offer of refuge made on Monday.
"We have no intention of looking for exile or asylum in the Dominican Republic, and even less in any country that oppresses its people," he said.

"With respect to the Cuban government's willingness to take us in, we consider it appropriate not to make a comment right now to avoid our words being distorted. We do this out of respect for the Cuban government, commander Fidel Castro, his revolution and his people."
In a surprise visit to Havana, President Alberto Fujimori announced on Monday Castro's offer to accept the roughly 20 rebels holding the residence since Dec. 17.
Castro confirmed he would accept the MRTA fighters out of a "moral duty" and "not a question of convenience." The MRTA draws its inspiration from the 1959 Cuban revolution.

The proposal drew immediate backing from Tokyo, whose cooperation is essential to any solution. Japanese officials said Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto would seek support from the United States, an avowed enemy of Cuba, for the proposal.
Top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama insisted the plan would be an effective way to resolve the crisis.
"I will not say whether this is morally right or wrong," Kajiyama told a news conference. "I think it is an effective way both in terms of not giving in to terrorism and of ending this peacefully."
Rebel leader Cerpa, however, said that Fujimori was creating "false expectations" with talk of an asylum and diverting attention from the main issue of the MRTA prisoners.

The government has flatly ruled out any releases, although Fujimori has offered an asylum deal and hinted at other concessions that analysts say may include improved prison conditions and trial processes.

Cerpa said eight rounds of face-to-face negotiations between the MRTA and government negotiator Domingo Palermo had brought "no significant advances," although they had allowed for an open exchange of views.

"But we believe this (the talks) cannot continue indefinitely in the sense that they can get worn down and lose a certain level of legitimacy," he said, adding the lack of concrete progress prevented his attendance at the last round of talks on Monday.

The rebel leader acknowledged the talks were "an important experience for us" in enabling the MRTA to give the government its opinion on official economic and anti-subversive strategies and "also listen to what they say about us in a framework of cordiality."
Fujimori was due to meet Palermo later on Tuesday for a debriefing on talks with the MRTA, which are slated to continue on Wednesday at a safe house near the besieged residence.

Earlier on Tuesday the MRTA transmitted its morning routine of singing and exercises by walkie-talkie to listening reporters. The rebels were heard counting one to 10 in military fashion and chanting defiant slogans such as "We will conquer!" and "Tupac Amaru does not surrender!"
